title: Operating Systems
summary: The referee between your code and the hardware — it decides who runs, what memory they see, and when they're allowed to touch the disk, network, or each other.

blocks.markdown:
The OS is a privileged program that shares scarce hardware among many programs and keeps them from wrecking each other.

- **Multiplexes the CPU** across many threads via scheduling.
- **Gives each process a private address space** backed by RAM through paging.
- **Guards the hardware** behind system calls that flip from user mode to kernel mode.
- Everything else is just detail on those three jobs.

blocks.subTitle: Why it exists
blocks.markdown:
The OS wasn't designed top-down — real constraints forced each feature into being.

| Pressure | OS answer |
|---|---|
| CPU precious, I/O slow | Scheduling |
| Memory finite, shared | Virtual memory |
| Code can't be trusted | Kernel mode + syscalls |

Multiprogramming — run others while one waits on I/O — created all three problems at once.

blocks.subTitle: Processes vs threads
blocks.markdown:
A process is the container for a running program; a thread is what the scheduler actually runs.

- A **process** owns a virtual address space, file descriptors, and at least one thread.
- A **thread** is a program counter, registers, and a stack.
- **Threads in a process share memory** (heap, globals, code); **processes do not** by default.
- Creating a process is expensive (clone the address space); a thread is cheap. Sharing needs locks; isolation needs IPC.

blocks.subTitle: A process's memory layout
blocks.markdown:
The kernel carves each address space into four regions, low to high.

- **Text** — read-only machine code.
- **Data/BSS** — initialized and zero-init globals.
- **Heap** — `malloc`/`new` allocations, grows up; you or a GC must free it or you leak.
- **Stack** — call frames and locals, grows down; freed automatically on return.

The free gap between heap and stack is why runaway recursion eventually overflows the stack.

blocks.subTitle: Context switching
blocks.markdown:
To run another thread the OS saves one thread's registers and restores another's.

- **Direct cost** is small — roughly **1–5 microseconds**.
- **Hidden cost** is bigger: the new thread's data isn't in caches, and a process switch may flush the **TLB**.
- Memory accesses stay slow until caches warm up again.
- Too many threads means you spend more time switching than working.

blocks.subTitle: CPU scheduling
blocks.markdown:
The scheduler picks the next ready thread and for how long. **Preemption** lets a timer interrupt forcibly pause a thread so none can hog the CPU.

- **Round-robin** — equal fixed quantum in turn; fair but blind to priority.
- **Priority** — high-priority first; risks **starvation**, fixed by **aging**.
- **MLFQ** — start high, sink CPU-bound threads, keep interactive ones up.
- Linux **CFS** runs whoever has accumulated the least runtime.

blocks.subTitle: Virtual memory & the TLB
blocks.markdown:
Each process gets a private virtual address space; the **MMU** translates virtual to physical in **4 KB pages**.

- **Page tables** in RAM hold the virtual→physical mapping.
- The **TLB** caches recent translations: a hit is ~1 cycle, a miss walks the page table.
- A **page fault** fires when a touched page isn't resident — the OS loads it and restarts the instruction, costing **millions of cycles**.
- This is what lets you run programs bigger than RAM. It's caching, one layer down ([caching](caching)).

blocks.subTitle: User mode, kernel mode, syscalls
blocks.markdown:
User code can't touch hardware directly — it asks via a system call.

- **User mode** runs ordinary instructions; **kernel mode** can do anything.
- A **syscall** loads a number and args, runs a **trap** instruction, and the CPU jumps to a fixed kernel entry point.
- The kernel validates, performs the work, then returns to user mode.
- It's the **only doorway** to hardware, costing hundreds of ns to a few µs — far more than a plain call, so **batch I/O**.

blocks.subTitle: From exec() to exit()
blocks.markdown:
A shell `fork()`s a child, which `exec()`s the target binary.

```c
pid = fork();          // child: copy-on-write copy of the parent
if (pid == 0)
    exec("./prog");    // replace image; new text+data mapped lazily
wait(&status);         // parent reaps the child's exit code
```

- `exec` tears down the old space, maps the new binary (pages load on demand via faults), and jumps to the entry point.
- On `exit` the kernel frees memory and leaves a **zombie** holding the exit code until the parent `wait()`s.

blocks.subTitle: Processes vs threads vs async
blocks.markdown:
Pick the concurrency model by what the work actually needs.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Fault isolation | Processes |
| Cheap switching, shared data | Threads |
| Huge I/O-bound concurrency | Async / event loop |
| CPU-bound on N cores | ~N threads |

Isolation buys safety but slow IPC; sharing buys speed but needs locks. Thousands of threads just thrash the scheduler.

blocks.subTitle: Page size & lazy work
blocks.markdown:
Two more axes you tune deliberately.

- **Small pages (4 KB)** waste less memory but need more TLB entries; **huge pages (2 MB)** cut TLB misses for big workloads but waste memory and slow fork.
- **Lazy vs eager**: demand paging and copy-on-write `fork` defer work for fast startup, but the first touch of each page pays a fault.
- High page-fault or swap activity means you're **memory-bound** — add RAM, not CPU.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & signals
blocks.markdown:
OS mechanics decide real architectures.

- **Linux CFS** runs the thread with the least `vruntime` from a red-black tree — fairness without hand-tuned queues.
- **Chrome** runs each tab in its own process: an exploit can't cross the address-space boundary.
- **Redis** serves on one event-loop thread — in-memory ops are µs-fast, so it dodges locks and switches ([caching](caching)).
- Watch: context switches/sec, major page faults, swap in/out, user vs system vs iowait CPU.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and prod:

- **"Threads always run in parallel."** Only with multiple cores; a GIL (CPython, Ruby MRI) blocks CPU-bound threading.
- **"Virtual memory just means disk as RAM."** It's fundamentally address translation and isolation; swap is one feature.
- **"A syscall is like a function call."** It crosses the privilege boundary and costs far more.
- **"More threads is always faster."** Past core count it adds switch and lock overhead.
- **"Page size doesn't matter."** It's a real TLB-vs-fragmentation trade-off.
